en: NAK 5-37 = NGMPP A 138/10, Part 3, following an anonymous exegetical fragment, after a continuous section very similar to [the preceding].
To be collated: • An apograph by MBB = MBB-I-42 ‘Prajñāvatāraṇayoga’ • Takaoka manuscript 51-2.
In the third [chapter] of the *Catuṣpīṭha* tantra, by means of the first [section],
one obtains its application, especially through the reality of mantra (4.1). This compendium is the essence of essences of the Dharma, known as the reality of the essence (*sāratattva*).
Then, for one who is extremely hidden [in practice], there is the application of knowing the reality; 4.2.
Having grasped the two [elements] from the son of the Guru, one should perform the pressing together like the moonlight at the head, which is the arising of the primordial seed. 4.3.
The tip of the tongue of one whose complexion is like a white jasmine or the moon is joined with the best [place].
One should fulfill the mantra recitation by means of the measures of the vowels during the reduction;
for the three previous rites, it is according to the syllables of the Guru.
The fourth [element] is also pure, consisting of white and yellow jewels.
Akula is the supreme Māla(nsuṃ), each subsequent state being higher than the last. The yogin should perceive the state of the garment and that which is beyond the garment.

Victory! The white mustard seeds and the unbroken *bandhūka* flower dissolve into the staff-thunderbolt (*daṇḍavajra*) that has been visualized according to the ritual procedure beginning with "eternal" (*nityādi*).
Having pressed the head with the moon, it is bathed through the state of non-duality. 4.6–4.7.

Having diligently bathed the lotus, vajra, and moons with nectar, [one should contemplate] the pervasive vowels and the all-pervasive syllable. Of the most excellent seed-syllables, it is the dark, pure, and lusterless *ma*. 4.8.
The seed of the action has three [syllables], while those of the four [others] never have four;
just as for the former end, due to the specific nature of the vowel-seed, so too for the end of the *agrendu*-seed, the preceding [part] is doubled. 4.9–4.10.

The four [elements] are indeed in equal proportion, joined with equal formative activity (*saṃskāra*). Three and four belong to the seed; thus is the bodily [nature]. (4.11) All [these] belong to the body of syllables by virtue of their innate nature and accent.

One should press upon the *akuśa* [syllable], as well as all the syllables of the body and the body-letters. 4.12. Especially for one who has conquered the yogin of the seed-syllables such as red and black, [one should do so] with the eight creatures in the fifth [house], and likewise the syllable in all ten [houses]. 4.13.
That which is called white, yellow, and red, as well as red, black, and light—

all these are of the nature of sound (*nāda*) for the purposes of pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and so forth. All ritual actions of this [mantra] are proclaimed according to the four castes.

The seed of *saptamuṣṭā* and so forth, along with human excrement and one's own [semen], [should be used]. 4.15. Likewise, for those who are paralyzed or auspicious, it is pressed with the seed of *maddhi*; [this] should be applied to all [cases] of the mild, red, well-formed, and black [types of poison] by the formidable one.
Nearby, joined with the remainder of the pillar-rites,
the two [syllables] of the *akuśa* seed are the nature (*prakṛti*) designated as syllables.
For the sake of the rite, they are for the purpose of piercing this seed-syllable of the reality of karma.

The divine red-colored radiance is like the seed of the power of subjugation (*vaśya*). One should dye one's own mental seeds with all the means for attaining success (*siddhi*). With neuter external seeds, one should [perform the rite] using the seeds prescribed in the *Dhruva* teachings. 4.18.

Indeed, that should be employed by both woman or man. [The first four syllables of each group are used], excluding the final four of the groups. One should know the ten syllables of the day; thus ends the tenth chapter. 4.19–4.20.
At the end of the fourth, in the group of five, the sixth is without continuity;
it is known as the "dust" (rajas), entirely empty, and does not indicate anything by way of distinction.
4.21. It is the immortal, the seed-syllable *nam*, with a luster equal to white jasmine.
For him, all principles are nectar; everything is accomplished. (4.22) He strikes down even the gods, siddhas, dānavas, and humans;
he brings about the downfall of all [opposing] actions through the specific nature of the seed-principle. (4.23)
Having visualized the two male gurus in the form of a chain-kiss, the light accomplishment of the one whose nature is virtue (guṇamala) is attained; one should place the nectar upon the head. 4.24.
The bindu is blazing above, divine; it is to be divided into four types.

The body consists of the five Buddhas, with the supreme seed-syllables of the five Buddhas; at the root and tip of the tongue, it is said to have a radiance equal to the color white. For pacifying rites, such as oblations and water rituals, those [syllables] are joined with the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The root-sound (mūlanāda) is said to be the middle vowel between 'a' and 'ī'.
For whichever deity's body one desires, specifically for rites of pacification (śāntika), it is taught that from the heart, the root-sound has a radiance equal to the color yellow.
4.27. From the heart, the root-sound is taught to have a luster identical to the color yellow.
By means of the sounds of the guru and the drops (bindus), together with the fires of the stomach and their functions,
[one attains] at the navel the resonance of the Ghorā [vowels] with a radiance equal to the color of blood.
One should employ the drawing-in of the rain through the yoga of the guru-sound.
At the tip of the [central] mark, the wise one should project a light of blue color and subtle sound, as previously described;
having bound the *cātana* and *māraṇa* [mantras], he should strike the wicked ones with the *kīla*.
One should employ the *cchik* and *huṃ* sounds for the concluding rites (*balikarma*) and so forth of Kṛṣṇa (4.31).
The four principles (*tattva*) of the principle are the *huṃ* sound as the protection of form;
all seeds belong to the most excellent one, and the *huṃ* sound possesses five characteristics (4.32).
Hūṃkāra is the supreme deity; Hūṃkāra is the vessel of accomplishment. Hūṃkāra is indeed emptiness; Hūṃkāra—to you, homage! 4.33

The application of the mixed existence and non-existence of that which is empty of form belongs to the one with the color of molten gold; the resonance, however, is the Meru-maṇḍala mountain. [34] Staying... [34]

Of the gods, asuras, siddhas, humans, and pure yoginīs, one should cause them to tremble with the entire body; this trembling is declared through the seed-syllable. [35] The moving [syllable] is the letter *ra* of the previous seed-syllable, constricted at its root.
The moon-light above and below is arranged with its points directed downward;
it is yellow in color, and these hooks are to be applied to the heart of the one to be mastered.
One should attract everything by means of the hooks, arising from the seed-syllable of the hook.
The seed-syllables of wind are the eight groups beginning with *ma*, located in the east;
at that time, they are pressed upon the roots, while the lunar drop (*candrabindu*) is at the crest.
One should impel the terrible color of wind into all embodied beings.

The seed-syllable of the impelling karma and so forth is elaborated from the reality of the seed. Of the third letter of each of the five groups, three syllables are taken; these three syllables are to be pressed together, yet separated from the root *repha*. [39–40]
One should extract the *Amṛtabindu*, which possesses a luster equal to the color of white;
it is the seed-syllable for the rites of pleasing and so forth for all bodies.
From the third letter of the first group, the root of the resonance (*nāda*) is hidden within the *ali*.
The Amṛtabindu is above, blazing with white luster.
[42] At the time of the ritual procedure for worship, [one performs] external fire-offerings and so forth with mudrās;
for the fulfillment of all rites, the seed-syllable PŪRAṆA is proclaimed. [43]
With the fourth of the first group, the root of the sound *ra*,
and the remainder, one should extract the blazing one, equal in radiance to the color of blood. It is devoid even of the fourth of the foremost of all actions.
That which is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of delusion for the entire body [is as follows]:
the third of the fifth group is taken with two syllables;
it begins with two voids and ends with a radiance equal to the color white. [45–46]
One should establish the gods, dānavas, guhyakas, and so forth, in their own desired locations.
The wise practitioner of ritual action (karmayogin), having performed the installation, should contemplate the perishable;
he should observe the void and its categories, and perform the gathering at its crossroads.
The nectar-drop (amṛtabindu) of the root syllables beginning with *gu*, *ru*, *puṃ*, and *sā* is drawn upward;
it possesses a radiance equal to the color white for one whose karma has been purified by fear and passion,
and it is the red reality (*raktatattva*) of the seed-syllable that brings about the realization of reality for yogins.

But by means of the threefold mantra, there is the division of syllables for the white, yellow, and red [mantras]; with three [syllables] of the red one... (33r/104r) [50]. Having taken the seventh final syllable, the month of the eighth is threefold.
Seated upon the seat of nectar (amṛtāsana), possessing a radiance equal to white in color; O Neuter One, manifest the seed-syllables! O Agni, be intensely radiant!
[With] the seed-syllables of the flame of fire... [51-52]
In the nourishing rite (*pauṣṭika*), having struck with the staff of sound, one offers the final oblation.
[54] His blood is nectar, along with that of the eight *pārśaraṇḍaka* birds;
all are offered with the blood of the *śaktara*, using the staff of *muntada* and *maukaśa*. [55]
In the recitation (*japa*), by means of the *hāra* and *svāsa*, the consciousness is drawn into the center.
For yogins, there are three types of red rites (*rakta-karma*); the syllable of the oblation (*huta*) is twofold. To know the syllable of destruction (*ghāta*), the fourth rite is now described.
One should perform the slaying through the utterance of the *tambhana* (paralyzing) mantra, or by means of the cause of binding.
The second section, consisting of the voids (*śūnya*), is joined to the side; the third section, consisting of the days (*dina*), is likewise on the side in its first half. [57–58]
One should visualize the seed-syllable as blue-colored, most terrible, endowed with rays like fire, and equal to a vajra-flame; one should pierce it with devotion.
For the purpose of killing, one should scatter the wicked seed-syllable everywhere for one who performs fierce rites.
For the yogin who desires accomplishment at the end of the syllables of destruction, [there are] his seed-syllables when joined; first, it is devoid of the staff and so forth;
at the end is *ātman*, which is increased and then halved, blue in color, and very sharp. [60–61]
For one who is wicked through incantations (*cāṭana*) or causing enmity (*udveṣa*), one should employ the blazing of the deity of wrath;
however, one should join its seed-syllable with the final syllable of *ghāṭa*.
One should take each preceding letter from the white class and the other classes.

The vajra-seed, however, is mastered from the seed-syllable *ṭa*. Having impelled the upward consciousness from its previous time, one should impel that syllable into the entry at the base of the navel. [63–64]
Of that supreme eightfold [mantra], one should recite the syllables with the *sītā* [vowels];
the time for the accomplishment is marked by the appearance of grey hair, preceded by the sign of a meteor (*ulkā*).
Prior to the sign of the meteor, the *yoginī* remains undistracted.
The seed-syllable of the *ūrṇā* and the grey hair (*palita*) is indeed purification or the imperishable (*akṣara*).
The *nāda* and *bindu* are joined to the seed-syllable of existence and non-existence.
The root-places of the wind are described by the expression "sound and the soundless" (*nādanāda*). [66–67]
When does the life-span of those abiding in the flower proceed by means of its seed?
For one whose mind is equanimous and who has previously practiced yoga, meditation, and so forth, there is bondage.
[68] There are seven ends of the seed; it is struck by the thunderbolt in the Immortal.

Having scattered the spots on the forehead like *kalpa*-flowers, one should take three syllables for each of the third letters of the respective classes. One should encircle the staff-like vajras with a girdle and so forth. [69–70]
[It is] the most excellent among the best;
it is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of the pure one by means of the three vehicles.
Of the third letter of the group of eight *ma*s, the goad (*aṅkuśa*) is pressed upon its head.
The radiance of the red object is divine, with a lunar drop as its crest.
[72] That which is joined to the principles from the navel...
the seeds named "Good Delusion" (sanmoha) are employed for the karma of delusion. [73]
Adorned on the head with the eight-pointed *vicabī* [mantra], which is the goad for the primary karma of delusion.
The roots of the seed, brilliant with a blue color, are at the base of the letter *ra*. [74] For all rites, one should employ scents, flowers, juices, and so forth;
one should strike the seeds of the name and destroy the actions (*karma*). [75]
The seed-syllable of *Sita* (Amitābha) has seven endings and possesses a radiance equal to a conch shell or a jasmine flower.
The seed-syllable of *Amṛtāmba* is known as *amba askara*.
The seed-syllable joined with *kaṣākṛ* possesses a radiance equal to yellow in color.
The syllable *ma* is proclaimed as the fire of the net (*jāla*), characterized by the imperishable (*akṣara*).

[77] Because it possesses the nature of the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*) of the preceding group of eight, the seed-syllables of wind are red; thus they are proclaimed as the seed-syllables of wind. [78]

The seed-syllable of the eighth [element], possessing a radiance equal to the color blue, resides in the heart of the earth; this is due to the earth-element-nature of that seed. Within this seed, there is a drop (*bindu*), which is the syllable at the root.

The two secrets are at the root of the letter *ra*; threefold is the root of the soundless (*anāda*) seed-syllable of wind. When the four drops are joined above, they constitute the four feet of the seed-syllable, which consists of six syllables.
The seeds of delusion are stirred by the winds of the seed-syllables;
for the purpose of joining the animal with fire upon the ground that has become a drawing, one should contemplate the eight yoginīs within the seed-syllable of eight finger-breadths. [82]
The principles of the self belong to the Supreme One, who cuts through the entire cycle of existence.
[83] With his head, he bears all beings; he is the imperishable one of all.
Having gathered his seeds, they are known as the seeds of gnosis. [84]

The eternal roots of the yellow [syllable], joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, are of the color of the white *kunda* flower and the moon, arising from the seeds of knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*).
In the cause, the seed is the controller; the seed is supreme beyond that.
The seed-syllable of knowledge should indeed be applied to all rites according to its name.
For the Bodhisattvas and others who are gentle, peaceful in form, and possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*),
one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth for as long as it takes until the end.
For a deity who is of dual nature, the female deity (devatī) is not joined;
rather, by means of the previous [deity] without a staff, there is then the consecration of the mantra for the deity or the female deity of the wrathful form, such as the jar and so forth. [88]
One should cause the *ghāṭa*, *ahara*, and so forth to be fashioned for the Vādī.
[89] Specifically, by means of "form and form" (*rūpa-rūpa*) for the state of being, and "anger and anger" (*krodha-krodha*), the seeds (*bījānām*) are distinguished by the *hutadhyābhadi*. [90]
Examine the principles of reality for everything through thorough investigation;

however, it is said that if one is established in what is not reality, accomplishment is far away. One should recite the seed-syllable of the deity, which is the form of the object to be accomplished.
The equanimity of that supreme one extends from the beginning, preceded by the gods, to the end; [92] the seed-syllable of the Vajra of the god Krodhakrodha is indeed with the vowels (an-dik-ai);
the goddess is for all beings, ending with the syllable of immortality (amṛtākṣara). [93]
The measure for that preceded by mantra is one less [than the standard];
for the self-syllables and the seed of the friend, there is examination due to the two causes.
For the seed of the void and the non-void, the middle [measure] belongs to the deity to be accomplished.
The preceding syllables constitute the means of accomplishment for that which is to be accomplished;
the yogi should cast aside the things to be accomplished of that rite. The practitioner of mantra must carefully investigate these in the times prior to the observation.
On the day of the void, death occurs at midday without a doubt.
Day by day, one should accomplish the day; the void is indeed the middle.
By the reversal of the seed-syllables, one should contemplate the remaining syllable.

If the remainder falls on a day, it is to be accomplished; if on a debt (the second lunar mansion), it is easily accomplished. If the remainders are zero, it belongs to the Sādhya [mansion]; if on Aḷi, it is fruitless.
One should examine this with great discernment; thus, through mantra-recitation, the success of the mantra is attained.
The neuter [mantra] of the previous seed-syllable, as well as the neuter to be accomplished, should be known as the essence of the flavors; this is what is called the *nina*.
With these four, one should accomplish the seed-syllable of one's chosen deity.
One should distinguish the name of the person for whom the rite is performed as the middle [syllable], while the preceding [syllables] are superior;

one should especially distinguish the deities of the middle [syllable] according to the specific application of the seeds of ritual logic for rites such as pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi). [101–102]
The sound of the letter *ra* from the root of the second *ra* in the void (*śūnya*),
a light above the moon, blazing with a yellow color—
this is the heart-essence of the names of all the yoginīs and deities, the supreme heart.
The prostrations for the designation of the name are at the end by those who are near.
[104] It is endowed with the specific [syllable] at the end of that which has its beginning and end removed;
it is marked with the letter *m* by means of the vowel *e* in the second section of the Śūnyavarga. [105]
At the base of the letter *ra*, with a drop (*bindu*) having a radiance equal to the color white, satisfy all the *yoṇīs* like the seed of the act of satisfaction.
All the principles (*tattvas*) of the seed belong to the Yoginī. || 106 ||
Then, specifically joined according to the sequence of the ritual manual,
with canopies spread out and fragrant mandalas,
one should offer worship and oblations with the scent of heaps of flowers and the like.
Having performed the various rites of mantra and mudrā, and having offered the material *bali* oblation, the wise yogin should draw the central enclosure with fragrant saffron;
he should then skillfully draw a square within the field of the grid. [108–109]
For Indra indeed established the syllable at the crown of the head;
the seed of that which is endowed with existence yet devoid of it is in the middle.
All those syllables of the day should be established according to their respective locations on the ground.
One should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the remaining eight groups, concentrated in mind;
it should be joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and possess a radiance equal to the color of blood.
Guggulu, indrasurasa, sohinin, sambha, nivālā, and śatā. [112]
Sihlaka, campaka, kunduru, koli, sothika, manahśila, aguru, kaṣṭha, sedurva, mada,
and madagandhaliptanta, combined with candana and rocanā— [113].
One part each of all-clove, nutmeg, sandalwood, saffron, and claw-nail [is to be added];
[114] in all storehouses and locations, this sequence of medicinal substances is established toward the direction of Indra.
Each one must be viewed individually; one should not cause the seed-portion to be lost. [115]
One should arrange one hundred and eight oblations ending with the word *praṇama*;
being intent on the application of the seed-syllable beginning with *bhava* and joined with the letter *m*,
one should employ the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) combined with *guggulu* and other substances.
But the king’s wife, O Indra among kings, being discerning, should be made to pay her share;
she who was consecrated by the sacrifice of five hundred leaves for the sake of the fivefold self-nature,
according to the fullness of each individual state as it was before.

Behold, O Brāhmaṇa! Whether it be a Śūdra, a woman, or a man, one should cause them to pay the prescribed portion of edible goods for one who is intoxicated, afflicted, or insane; this is the rule established by the vintner. [119] This is the vow.

Now, for those of low birth who are to be brought under control, one should skillfully employ the following medicinal herbs: *modā* and others, along with human oil, in equal proportions; having observed these ingredients, they should be prepared with great care. [120–121]
Entering the royal palace, or suffering defeat in legal proceedings—
by means of this, one should give that which deludes the world.
(122) Sugar and other substances, combined with sandalwood, are for the former case.
One part of *varga* and one part of sandalwood—[123] a yogin should smear this upon his limbs and so forth in the presence of those he desires;
by the mere scent of the fragrance, even one who is unwilling shall come under his control. [124]

Having taken [the substance] from the Madhupākṣa region, one should fumigate the state of another; thus, being powerless, one gains power over all. Having gathered it with Naṣika, it is joined with a portion of sugar.
With incense, with incense, through incense, there shall be the enchantment of men.
One should contemplate Jñānaḍākinī situated in the center of the lunar mandala;
the individual seed-syllables of the seed-mantra are one hundred and one in every respect.
This powder is black when intoxicated, yet it is indeed red in color.
Having gathered its substances with those whose essence is the goddess Jñānadevī, [it is prepared];
by means of Sūryapāṇi, it possesses a radiance equal to the color of blood.
The seed-syllables of reality are [produced] by means of moving and causing to fall.
One should contemplate the solar disc situated in the center of the mandala within the heart;
in the middle of that, among the seed-syllables, is the bindu of the letter *ra*.
By performing the shaking and the casting down with the joined recitation,
and subsequently through the rite of offering (bali), the entire world of moving and unmoving beings is brought under control.
One should employ guggulu, the five insects, and the hundred roots.
Within a subtle egg of the wind element, they die immediately and swiftly.
[132] One should cause seven stable insects, such as those belonging to the category of *gītabhāga*, to consume [the target];
after consuming for seven nights and so forth, they die—of this there is no doubt. [133]
One should protect the five types of insects from Śoñcika with the five [substances] of Unmatta and Mamba;
one must die among those who eat with their hands, and such a person becomes insane. One should nourish all the insects of Medapāñca with eggs.
Even a mere drop of this elixir, when consumed, causes one to die from leprosy in an instant.
[135] The group of sugar-candy insects is joined with *goli* and *maṇḍaka*;
for those who consume its powder, men are deprived of their voices. [136]
Having taken *śarkara* and *koṇya*, one should saturate them with honey and clarified butter;
by consuming the powder thereof, colic is instantly destroyed. [137] Having taken *nakhi* (? and *koṇya*, one should saturate them with honey.
With water and hands immediately after consuming even a minute amount of food,

the wise one who knows the sequence of the land should examine the scripture— the most profound meaning of the application of the essence of reality— for the sake of the realization of the knowers. [138–139]
[He is] not stained by sin through [the acts of] those who revile the Three Jewels, the preceptor, or the secret [teachings], according to the words of all the Yoginīs.
Thus ends the *Pañcapañcikakramanirdeśa*. Om.
Now, [the teaching] regarding the specific [practices] of the *krodha* [deities],
which are the most excellent of all, the essence of the essence of reality (*tattva*),
for one who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, is the sequence of the ritual procedure for worshiping the mantras. [141]
The *balikarma*, the true reality (*tattva*), and the placement of the scented chamber (*gandhakoṣṭha*) and so forth;
[142] the placement of the square chamber for that which is...;
one should place the head at the end of the group of vowels beginning with the void of the day and ending with *kavajra*. [143]

Indra and the others are for the location, preceded by their respective vowels in due order; the placement of the seed-syllable begins with all the squares, starting with *ma* and ending with *oṣadhā*.
[144] *Nakhi*, *vāla*, *viṭaga*, *maṭa*, *guṭa*, and *vāsaka*.
One should place wood and other materials in the seven locations starting from the northeast.
[145] Indra-hasta, vacā, kuṣṭha, go-mohani, candravāri—these are the seven; they should be placed in equal parts in the second position. [146]

The group of crystal and non-crystal substances consists of saffron, gorocana, and honey as the seventh part; these are placed in the third set of compartments. [147] The compartment for resinous substances consists of sarja, guggulu, fragrant substances, sugar, and kunduru.
In the fourth [stage], one should place seven *jātī* flowers at each station;
[148] for those whose lotuses have faded, *kākoli*, *kesara*, and *koñci* are used in hundreds of thousands.
In the fifth, it is proclaimed that one should apply a seventh part. [149]
Gandha, gandhārākṣāra, harītāla, harīhaka, honey, and a portion of pippalī; the sixth is koṣṭha and also koṣṭhaka. Danti, dantā, kusumbha, nelikā, smāri, and cetakī.
The seventh part of the essence, however, consists of the sequence of the seven medicinal herbs.
A hundred minus half of the deficient [portion] constitutes all the medicinal herbs for the storehouse and so forth;
each one of the mantra is also well-composed as a hundred.

O King of kings, one should have skilled artisans prepare a fine powder of the seven groups of substances beginning with *nakhi* and ending with *kṛṣṇa*, each consisting of seven parts; then, O Lord of kings, one should offer this collection as a gift for the feet and so forth.
Everything comes under one's control everywhere through the power of one’s own will.
[154] One should have a fine powder made from the color of Indra’s hand;
having taken this powdered substance, one should mix it seven times with one’s own saliva. [155]
If one, being well-composed, causes [the powder] to be given according to the prescribed method of consumption,
then women or men will come under control everywhere. One part of rock crystal (sphaṭikā) from the aforementioned group should be ground into a fine powder.
Having combined it with human oil, dry it in the shade. When one who is fond of royal service applies this tilaka in the forenoon, one should know that good fortune will quickly come to pass.
One should have fine powders made from the group of substances beginning with *sarja*;
then, having added honey, sugar, and powdered sandalwood,
this preparation should be given to all three women for consumption.
...of Hrapasa, who was fortunate and longing for his beloved...
[161] As soon as this has been smeared, it may cause delusion through the power of liberation.
All the various classes of fragrances and so forth should be mixed with ghee and milk. [162]
One should cover it with every available portion and not let it dry out;
for those of low birth and other mlecchas who desire both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
one should cause the nectar-like, pure [medicine] to be administered when it has been prepared.

One should apply seven parts of *dantī* and seven parts of *rākṣā*; it should be joined with *karañja* and *guḍūcī* when the heat has subsided. One should win over the unloved by placing them in a beloved position and by addressing them with pleasant words.
By means of three sentences, bring the self of the sentence under the control of one's own will.
With the five waters, including that of a female elephant and a maiden,
one who is disciplined and liberated from the self shall manifest the state beyond [duality].
By means of incense—incense, incense—the practitioners perceive its fragrance.
The name of that body of the Mleccha and others is proclaimed as Vaśā.
[167] Having taken Saraṇā, one should have it made into a fine powder.
The *malayana* should be tied; one should cause it to be made part by part. One should examine the pure offering for the best rite of the medicinal herbs.
through the application of Vajrasattva, [it becomes] with the beautiful luster of molten gold.
Seated upon a lotus throne, he is the subduer of all embodied beings.

it burns with intense redness, drawing forth the consciousness of the one to be subdued. [172]
The vowels and *bindus* are doubled and joined with the root-sound (*mūlanāda*). Joined with the root-sound, this is named "Amṛtāntika"; it accomplishes the characteristic of subjugation (*vaśa*).
Having combined the medicinal herbs, one should prepare them with sandalwood at their center.

One should serve with hundreds of thousands and millions of offerings for the consecration of the reality of power (balitattva). [174] They go forth with full hands and limbs, endowed with a hundred drops;
one should cause edible substances to be given to men, excluding [unfit] persons. [175]
One should take *dantī* from the east and mix it with the insect and goat’s milk;
by merely eating this, one will be afflicted by deaths for seven days.
[176] With seven *kusumbha* insects, five *unmatta* fruits, and *mumbaka*...
[Whatever] edible [substance] there may be,
[mixed with] the root of the *nelivarga* plant and combined with white lead,
that edible thing should be cast down by everyone, including the quarrelsome. [177–178]
One should apply the *kasmarī* and the group of six [herbs] with human oil for one who is unfortunate or disliked; however,
one should cause a *cetakī* woman to win by means of a *maṇḍimaṇḍa* of the seven groups.
The Bindu-mantra of the food indeed causes instantaneous awakening;
however, for one who consumes twenty measures of the group beginning with *saṃralā* mixed with goat urine,
death will occur within twenty days, even if only a small amount is eaten.

The juice of the *dantikonī* and other insects mixed with honey and snake venom should be administered to one who eats food; it will cause pain in the limbs through leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). [182] One should cause the juice of the *saralarākonyaka* insect to be given to those who eat food.
By that, they remain in a state of distraction and lack meditative concentration, their delusion shattered.

For those who harm the Three Jewels and revile the Teacher and the Secret [Teachings], no sins exist, according to the words of all the Yoginīs.
Those of inferior wisdom, lacking intelligence, possess the latent tendencies of delusion, afflictions, and the like. [185]
The medicinal preparation for the *mantra-yogābhayas* proceeds [as follows].

Now, through the sequence of mantra yoga of the essence, the accomplishment of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* shall belong to those who seek its goal and have diminished afflictions. [5.1]
I shall accomplish the goal of that which has wisdom and skillful means as its root through my own intentional action.
Wisdom is that which illuminates knowledge, while skillful means is that which leads [beings]. This yoga has wisdom as its root; for the practitioner, ethical conduct serves as its support.
With the companion of wisdom, one should abandon the afflictions;
one should cast off the defects of existence, as well as pride, craving, delusion, and so forth.
Since the state of things is impermanent, one should therefore relinquish all conceptual notions.
If it were non-existent, it would not be a real entity; nor could that which has not arisen bring about cessation.
Furthermore, there is no abiding of a real entity; if one holds such a view, it is causeless.
[5.5] Existence, non-existence, and so forth are the extremes, while purity and impurity are the middle.
His characteristic is the recognition of signs, equanimity, and the possession of secrecy;
[5.6] it is liberated from the graspable and the ungraspable, and devoid of the notion of substantial entities.
Through the awakening of a Buddha, the essence of all beings is grasped by means of thorough investigation. [5.7]
Not grasping at existence, one should avoid the entity that is devoid of being;
joined with both existence and non-existence, one should perform the churning of milk by well-grasping it with the view of equality alone.
[5.8] And the understanding of the treatises, as well as consciousness, is considered to be the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The lineage of the middle state of the Ṛgveda is to be cultivated;
however, the lineage of the nature of knowledge is the locus of the sequence. By means of the positions impelled by the supreme, one places the pestle and the mortar in the hands. [5.10]
[He made] a collection of things according to his own will, such as the *urva* and *urvādi*, from the *māgāvya*.
For one who has conquered the seven Māras and the enemies of this saṃsāra, where could there be an enemy before him, when he has wisdom and skillful means as his companions? [5.11]
Laziness, sleep, desire, anger, and delusion are [overcome] by those who are vigilant.
[5.14] Hunger afflicts the body; it consumes one's vital energy and brings about all faults, including indolence.

One who is skilled in sleep remains in the body, which is the vessel for the fall into existence; [5.15] having cast out agitation and having crushed the affliction of the mind, one’s own desire is the intention regarding the object.
Indeed, by whatever means of pride one’s own desire and thought are applied with effort, [5.16]
[5.17] This is the compendium of the essential points for beginning the practice of the Yoginī.
Having firmly formed the vajra-añjali gesture, one should make the aspiration for those who perform the supreme deeds.
[5.18] Oṃ! All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
All phenomena are purified by yoga; I am purified by yoga.
Having made a vow for the sake of all excellence, that deity is with objective support.

One should produce that consciousness according to one’s own will, free from craving, delusion, and the like. [5.21] It stands in the center of a lunar disc, adorned with the body of Māmakī; it is the play of the five Buddhas, with a radiance equal to a white *kunda* flower or the moon. [5.22]
With two arms, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, holding a vajra and a bell joined together,
his body adorned with all ornaments, and emitting rays of blazing fire— one should meditate upon him as non-conceptual and unassailable through the state of meditative cultivation.
By means of application at the improper time, the seed is raised by the seed-seeds; [5.24] the measure is the end of the oblations, through the recitation according to one's own desire with the mind.
Subsequently, there is cessation in sequence, well-composed in selflessness. [5.25]
All forms are the divisions of this [reality], which is non-conceptualized through the three realms;
it is not like the moon and so forth, for its emptiness is the omniscience of all things.
Emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and the great emptiness—the cultivation of existence by means of existence.
For him whose remaining thirst has been extinguished, who is wise and radiant, who is unshakable and unassailed by the state of existence through the state of non-existence—
for him, by the illumination of his rays, the stars within the three realms [are outshone]. (5.28)

The wise, having perceived the throbbing radiance and the blazing expansion, realize the middle way of existence, non-existence, and so forth, as well as form and formlessness; they see his constant state, which is both with and without conceptual designation. [5.29]
Having characterized the characteristics of this [meditation]— which is empty of form and so forth, and which possesses a beginning, middle, and end—
one should cultivate it with well-composed mind through the sequential application of cessation. Furthermore, there is no pain in the limbs and so forth, nor does the mind become agitated.
The gradual and non-gradual commencement, the piercing of the joints and the piercer—[5.31] one should teach the sequence of awakening for the mind regarding the eternal principles;
indeed, one should observe its yoga of thorough investigation and integration. [5.32]
Oṃ vattali 2 śvetamukhi huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
[5.33] One should recite this mantra and the true reality through the application of Jñānaḍākinī.
[Her form is] complete with beauty, possessing a radiance like molten gold. [5.34]
Seated in the lotus posture, with vajra-rays raised upward, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times through the yoga of gnosis and the mind.
Thereafter, one may undertake the ritual activities; the details regarding enjoyment and liberation are extensive.
Having collected funeral ashes and so forth, one should draw a mandala on a vessel. Within that, a stepped mandala is fashioned from charcoal powder,
square with four gates and adorned with four archways.
Having drawn five in the center, adorned with eight *kapālas*,
one should offer the essence of the offering (*balitattva*) consisting of the true nature of perfumes such as incense and so forth. All things for enjoyment are vast and manifold objects of worship.
One should attract [the deities] with the Jñāna-Ḍākinī, surrounded by the four messengers:
Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Curṇikā in the four directions.
Everything, by everything, and all things, should be worshipped with a mind of equanimity.
At that site, which is the beginning of all things, one should cause the fire-ritual and other rites to be performed.
As for the remains of the funeral wood, they are the very tree of his banner.
Having diligently ignited the fire for him with Mātaṅgī, one should kindle that fire.
And with excellent vajra-parrots mixed with honey and clarified butter, by offering them with the supreme mantra, the goddess becomes pleased;
yet she may manifest in various terrible forms amidst tumultuous, swirling, and fierce sounds. [5.42–5.43]
One should not fear any location or region; one should employ the eightfold magic.
When the king with his fourfold army arrives swiftly, one should hurl an insult at him. [5.44]
In the treatment of the mind, Mount Meru is not a syllable, nor is it the beginning; what then is the earth that could be shaken?
There are various foul odors, yet they are not terrifying. [5.45]
Through a great resolve and ten thousand oblations, the yogin attains accomplishment;
there is no doubt in this matter, for the Gnosis-body is supreme.
Through the ritual action of the offering (bali), one accomplishes the activities of the mudrās of mantra.

For one whose [practice] is accomplished without dependence, there is no doubt in this matter. [5.47] One should show the Goddess to the others; offerings such as bali and arghya should be given, well-conjoined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). [5.48]
"What is this deep and magnificent roar? Which being has incensed me so that I may grant them their desired perfect accomplishment?
[5.49] Then the practitioner should say: "May you grant me perfect accomplishment."
O Great Yavīya, if you so desire, you shall grant me the boon:
"If doubt should arise regarding the Māras, the afflictions, the grahas, and so forth, [one should perform] a great oblation with a hook (*mahāṅkuśa*) combined with great oil. [5.50–51]
They are accomplished here, there is no doubt, by the word of Vajrasattva.
One should accomplish the supreme goddess, the bestower of all siddhis;
the wise one should accomplish her having renounced body and life. || 5.52 ||
Now, the supreme reality of gnosis is subtle, peaceful, free from objects of perception, all-pervading within every being, whether established or not;
yet, by means of the afflictions, the body is grasped through the impurities of existence and so forth. [5.53]
Wherein, by means of the mind of the body, sensation, and so forth, there is no portion of the place;
even in the twelve seasonal stations, the mind of the portion is formless.
By means of the station of delusion, the station is colored by the state of existence.
Through the severing of delusion and so forth, the yogin should abandon the five states of existence and the like, which are difficult to cast off.

He should strike at the notion of "self" as being like a jar covered by the skin of a pure lamp. With a pure body free from affliction, he should contemplate non-existence for one who is joined with existence, having realized that which is called evil-doing.

The ocean of the afflictions such as passion is difficult to grasp; [5.57] it always abides within the lotus of the twelvefold bases, consisting of ignorance and knowledge. With the companion of pure phenomena, one purifies the water that has been offered as a floral offering. [5.58]
The body of afflictions and the like have been severed by means of the distinctions of existence, the lotus, and so forth;
conceptual constructions, which are the cause of existence and most terrible, are [destroyed] like fire. For those yogins who desire the goal, conceptual construction stands at a great distance.
Having accomplished the mind of equanimity, he should show it to all. Established in the supreme, he should perform the ritual acts of perception and so forth, which are without characteristics.
He should taste the five nectars and offer the nectar as an ointment.

Having drunk the nectar, even in the absence of the eternal ones, one should draw in the five hooks by means of the imagined; thus the deity, the all-knowing of all deities, brings the Yogas, Ḍākinīs, gods, and so forth, swiftly under one's control through one's own self. [5.62]
One should always consume the great *vema* according to its true nature; other conceptualizations are merely mental constructs.
Having contemplated it as a liquid nectar, one should eat even the *maṅkuśa*.
By virtue of its eternally pure nature, it is free from both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
The pure body of the heroes is indeed of a pure nature; there is no doubt about this.

The yogin, having abandoned the distinction between those who may and may not be approached, should avoid [ordinary women] and take up [the practice with] those who are not of his own lineage, such as the Śākya women and others. [5.65] He should consort with the king and others.
Having placed his lotuses upon it, first there is the pure sign;
[5.66] then the leafless, pungent-smelling, and impure—these must be consumed with a pure disposition; thus the second sign is shown. [5.67]
Affection is the seal for all, never causing them any distress;
compassion toward all beings is the third sign that has been shown.
[5.68] But the resolve for renunciation, through constant effort, makes all things like blades of grass.
The fourth sign is shown by one whose mind is profound and noble:
being firm in the state of non-duality, pure, impartial toward a single task, and constantly devoted to the guru.
Vigor should be applied everywhere by those who possess patience toward generosity, ethical discipline, and the rest;
one should perform various firm meditations. Thus the sixth sign has been shown.
[5.71] Through learning, arts, and crafts, there is always equanimity of mind.
The seventh sign demonstrates the body that eternally acts for the benefit of sentient beings. [5.72] The Buddha awakens those sentient beings who are submerged in the mud of ignorance;
the eighth sign demonstrates the illumination of the path to perfect enlightenment. [5.73]
By no one at all—whether through substances, non-substances, or conceptualizers; nor by signs such as Māra or those corrupted by Māra—are conceptualizations of entities abandoned.
(5.74) When practiced with corrupt and fierce tantras, one does not attain success.
One should equalize the bodily practice of austerities with the dances of worldly existence through the mind of the assembly of phenomena;
one should not consume conceptual constructions, for that is the cause for the failure of yoga-siddhi.
The essence of churning is indeed the oil; the world with its mobile and immobile beings is the vessel for accomplishment.

The essence of that essence is the cultivation of the fire of the mind of gnosis through the practice of dharma. This excellence does not fall away, provided one follows the yoga scriptures over time.
In the eternal consciousness, may the stages of yoga, meditation, and ritual action be purified;
[5.78] through the yoga that precedes over-yoga, there is the great stage beyond yoga; indeed, these four activities are employed by the wise for the sake of transcending existence. [5.79]
The arising, the preliminary practice, the yoga of breath, and that which is established through the sequence;
the vital points, the mind, and so forth, the state beyond yoga, and the characteristics such as worship;
[5.80] the fire-mind and so forth are to be experienced, shown to be equal like the sun.

One should transform the olfactory faculty and the ear into the nature of wind for the sake of honoring sounds. [5.81] Those who perform worship should thoroughly understand the intrinsic nature of all things through their practice;
the rite of offering is performed with those [deities] according to what has been taught, through yoga that is non-dual. [5.82]
One should properly effect the union of existence and non-existence through those joined with the awakening of a Buddha and so forth;
indeed, Mahāmudrā is the means, known by the designations of Yoga and Atiyoga, which is born from the dharma of selflessness and is well-investigated within its own nature. [5.83]
The body is like a void and so forth; this is the fourth, the Great Yoga.
(5.84) Thus is the characteristic of all, the vow through the Great Mind. Activity proceeds eternally in saṃsāra and beyond it for the sake of bliss. (5.85)
With eyes like blue lotuses and a wide-open mouth,
one who enjoys the five objects of desire— partaking of pleasant food and pleasant touch—
should accomplish the visualization of bliss, having experienced all sensual pleasures.
But by means of conceptual construction, for yogins, through the turning of the wheel of cyclic existence,
the wise one, having sat comfortably upon a seat in a location favorable to the mind, should accomplish the nature of the Great Mind. [5.87–88]

The *saṃpuṭā* of the moon and sun, with the fingers bent at the joints like the rising of the sun and moon; the *dhūmā* mudrā, raising the three impurities, is proclaimed as the *sattvavajrī*. The *m-ākṣepa*, the *kīla*, the *prākāra*, and the *pañjara* are effective for all ritual actions.
One should display his seal, a splendor equal to a garland of flames.
[5.90] Between the wings of the bird is the crescent moon; the lord of serpents presses upon it, while the letter *ra* emits fire-flames from its head, made powerful by the night. [5.91]
The supreme state, eternally peaceful, possessing a radiance equal to a flame—
this seed-syllable, condensed by these [elements], is the accomplisher of all rites.
Having filled the body with sound, one should [visualize] form and so forth by means of the wings and other parts.
One should contemplate one's own body as seeds, leaving only the seed-remainder. [5.93] The limbs, which have been cast aside by the eight syllables, are endowed with all ritual actions;
they are the essences of the reality of emptiness, conjoined with the previously mentioned characteristics. [5.94]
One should not disparage the Tīrthikas, even if they are like parrots devouring food;
rather, one should maintain an equanimous mind toward the senses and the enjoyment of their objects.
Having previously made the vow for omniscience, one should strive for the fruit of the accomplishment of what is to be achieved.
Through that yoga of yogas, which is difficult to master, one should employ the vajra as the skillful means.
Having formed the two vajra-fists and held them at the region of the waist,
one should fill [the space] with the sound of the syllable *huṃ* and sing the song of accomplishment.
Ja ja ja ja! O Vajrasattva, grant the accomplishment of the descent!
Ha ha ha ha! O Lord of the *huṃ* syllable, may the pledge (*samaya*) be fulfilled! Uma ūnate! Va va va va! O Secret One of the Vajra-Explosion, the consumer of the oblation!

A A A A [A] he tovyava vajra alimakta sulīyana hūṃ! [5.98] By these songs, the great secret, all the yoginīs are delighted; with a mind focused on the foremost yoga, through the sweet sounds of the *kākalī* lute. [5.99]

The element of space, extending to all limits, is the middle among the three elements; may wind and space be accomplished by one whose mind is joined with the void. (5.100) One should meditate upon the moon mandala in the center of the wind mandala.

In its center, one should meditate with a well-composed mind upon the syllable *ali*, which is most beautiful and endowed with splendor, possessing the colors and other qualities of the ritual action.
The syllable *ali* is proclaimed to be the severance of both emanation and withdrawal. [5.101–5.102]
Just as for the third letters of each group, three *akula* syllables are taken;
on the sides of the staff, one should encircle it with white lotuses covering the vajras.
Having meditated upon these, the supreme yogin cuts through all of saṃsāra. [5.103]

Thereafter, the Great Being, the Holder of the Excellent Vajra, [visualizes] his own body as being completely filled with water, equal in number to eight [vases]. In its center, most beautiful, is a lovely white lotus. [5.104–105]
Situated in the center of the wind-maṇḍala, holding the seed-syllable of Duḥkhendra,
completely covered by a white lotus, and emitting manifold rays of light and flames—
from that, the syllable *ma* arose, consisting of the nature of Vajrasattva. [5.106]
[He is] white, with the color of a jasmine flower or the moon, two-armed, and adorned with a chest-ornament;
he is the playful one consisting of wisdom, seated upon a pedestal of the five elements.
With a vajra firmly held at his heart, he should place a bell at his left hip.

Adorned with all ornaments through the nature of passion and vigor, blazing with rays and colored by the hue of manifold states of being; possessing the brilliance of a diamond, quivering and sharp, it is filled with clouds of Buddhas. [5.109]
One should cultivate with the state of being, unwavering and unassailed,
the desired recitation of the yogins along with its cultivation, provided one possesses awareness; indeed,
for the one of the most excellent name, it is the middle, while *praṇama* is at the beginning and end.

The great six-syllable mantra is the source of all beings; for those engaged in recitation and meditation, their desired activities are accomplished according to their will. By practicing the three protections, the activity of the mind is perfectly accomplished. Om. [5.112]
Then, for one who has fallen into the danger of death due to the loss of all essential substances,
the non-dual yoga of knowledge is desired through the attainment of wisdom.
[5.113] One should [meditate upon] the vajra-bell, the true reality, and the non-dual form of the gnosis-body.
The vajra is held firmly in the hand, while the bell rests upon the level palm.
[5.114] The lotus should be joined with the vajra; that is the supreme binding of the mudrā.
With two hands, one should hold the bell at the neck, and with one [hand], one should press the vajra. One should not touch [it]. [5.115]
One should press the door of the left with the knowledge of the non-reality of the self;
one intent on the consciousness of duality should meditate through the state of being with being, from the space-element downwards, in the middle, and upwards. [5.116]
Emptiness is the refuge for all by one whose mind is well-investigated.
[5.117] The lamp-maker is the remainder; the seed-syllable *ali* is the middle one.
The garland of flames is very sharp, consisting of the three elements together with the assembly. [5.118]
Thereafter, having manifested the form with its two-fold beautiful nature,
one should accomplish the supreme state through the application of the Lord Daṇḍavajreśvara, whose abode is wisdom and the girdle, and who possesses the vajra-bell.
One should perform the recitation with the two organs joined in the secret vajra-pressing.
Having offered the vital breaths into the end of the seed-syllable of the liquor,
one should accomplish the eternal, supreme, and subtle state with a joyful mind.
The ritual procedure for mental worship, however, accomplishes everything through the mind. The yoga for the descent of the wisdom-vajra is completed. Om.
Then, one who follows the system of yoga should respectfully take up all the essences, which are the most excellent and supreme compendium;
it should be consumed with a pure disposition and a mind like a crystal. [5.122]

Cultivated with a pure disposition, one who is endowed with all the characteristics [should practice] for an eon; yet for the non-conceptualizing one, food and non-food are equal. For him who has transcended the world, there is no expectation, and he eats according to his own will. [5.123–124]
Having diligently gathered that [teaching] from the heroes who have previously received initiation and so forth,
through the sequence of months and the year,
one should likewise cultivate the four characteristics of the vow and their qualities.

Especially on the eighth day, on the full moon, and on the fourteenth day, one should diligently offer the bali-oblation; afterwards, the ritual sequence and the vow itself [should be performed]. All his ritual actions [are thus accomplished]. || 5.127 ||
