Thus, through all these mantras of truth, there is no doubt that this will be accomplished. By means of the yoga of the feast (gaṇacakra) involving food and so forth, one should seize the day of the final month. If one thoroughly contemplates the dharma as desired, all mantras will be accomplished. Whether possessing the ascetic observances (vrata) for each day, or even if they are not available, one should seize the days of the year during the final [fortnight] of the middle summer month. At night...

Just as it has been taught, having bestowed [the gift] with faultless mantras, one will at all times abide in glory and the seven excellences. Through delighting in yoga, the Dharma, and so forth, and being endowed with the most excellent non-dual companion, one should rely upon that Dharma and strive to attain the supreme state. By means of emptiness, form is destroyed, and the phenomena that were grasped are exhausted.

One should contemplate the sky of universal restraint with perfect meditative equipoise. Within the space of all things, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of the moon and milk. With many blazing rays of light, white in color like the *kunda* flower and the moon—the supreme and primary seed-syllable *āḥ*—one should meditate while the breath is unmoving. Through the application of a single moment, one becomes the nature of the Wisdom Ḍākinī, with three faces and [six] arms.

The sixth [deity] himself has light equal in color to blue; he sits in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, adorned with a sun-maṇḍala. Upon his head is a vajra-crest, and his head is adorned with the five Buddhas. He is fully adorned with laughter, wrath, and grace, and with three eyes. He wears a lower garment of elephant hide and is clothed in human skin. Of humans...

Completely adorned with all the bone ornaments of the five limbs, with hair-tips that are exceedingly soft, and a radiance equal to a blazing fire; in the first [right] hand he holds a *khaṭvāṅga*, in the second he brandishes a battle-axe, and in the third is a vajra. In the left hands, he makes the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and holds a noose; the second holds a skull-cup filled with blood, while the sword-hand is held above. He possesses vajra-rays that are stainless.

With clouds of Buddhas radiating forth, one should sport in the center of the earth; one should meditate on entities through entities. One should visualize vultures, jackals, lions, and tigresses in the cardinal directions; crows, owls, vultures, and *cāṣa* birds should be placed in the intermediate directions. Uttering terrifying sounds with bared fangs, they cause great alarm with the syllables *ha*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*. Thus is the sovereign queen of the ḍākinīs.

One should meditate upon oneself with the mind; having extracted [the deity] from one's own breath, one should place it within the reflected image and so forth. The yogi should visualize [the deity] in all its aspects within that location, such as in a painted image. Abiding in the state of desire and liberation, the non-dual deity of the *bali* offering is present. Through the gateway of application, the practitioner shall explain the ritual for this offering: the food, the feast, and reality itself.

Having performed the supreme secret offering, one should abide in the center of the maṇḍala of the heart. From the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, one should mentally generate its form and so forth, and manifest the identity of Vajrasattva. Having meditated upon the excellence of food and so forth as pure entities, through the practice of intense meditative equipoise, by means of this union for even a moment—*oṃ āḥ hūṃ hrīḥ svāhā*—it blazes with *oṃ*.

One should realize it through the aspect of *ba*, understand it individually through the aspect of *ha*, manifest it with the seed-syllable *ho*, and purify stains through the aspect of *hrīḥ*. Because the body itself is the deity, one should realize it through the aspect of *ā*. Through these five seed-syllables, the deity—the five Buddhas themselves—is fully absorbed. *Oṃ jvaṃ ghraṃ traṃ hūṃ āḥ svāhā*. By means of this mantra, one should take hold of the excellence of the food and so forth.

With the form of *BYA*, one should purify the body; with the form of *AŌṂ*, one should grasp it; with the form of *GHRAṂ*, one should fill the stomach; with the form of *TRĀṂ*, one should purify the stainless body; and with the form of *HŪṂ*, one should consume it. If the yogin constantly makes offerings to the syllable *A* at the heart with the mind, using perfumes, lamps, flowers, divine food (*naivedya*), and ritual cakes (*bali*), at the time of song—

Having prepared melodious songs and instruments such as the *vīṇā* and the flute, one should always worship with these sounds while reciting the identity of Vajrasattva. Whether walking, sleeping, sitting, or moving about—at all times and in every situation—the practitioner, with a focused mind, should constantly contemplate Vajrasattva. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā*. Through the application of the reflection of primordial wisdom (*jñāna-bimba*), this seed syllable is to be recited.

By performing this, all sins are cast far away and one’s own desires will be accomplished. Even for the sin arising from the five elements committed by one who has caused a secret to be disclosed, if one constantly meditates and recites [this], one will be liberated from all sins. *Oṃ kara kara prajñā mahā-tīkṣṇa pañca oṃ buddhe ha, oṃ krodha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, ā ā ā mu mu mu svāhā.* [Mantra]

This seed-syllable of the Great One is the condensed essence of the Buddha-mind. By the practitioner engaged in the faultless application, the seed-syllable endowed with all [qualities] is as follows: at the very end of the night and at the first hour of Rohiṇī, one should take two *māṣaka* of mercury from Magadha, place it in a vessel of *nīpa* wood, and visualize a full moon disk within it, perfectly situated in the midst of nectar; thus one should contemplate the nectar.

As for the method: when a yogi in profound meditative equipoise recites the mantra seven times over water and drinks it, all misdeeds are destroyed; the nectar of primordial wisdom and the body of primordial wisdom are attained; mindfulness, sharp intelligence, wind-energy (*vāyu*), majesty, and glory increase; one becomes entirely fortunate; and [one is freed from] hearing, wisdom, wealth, and the disorders of wind, bile, and poison.

This water removes all diseases caused by wind, phlegm, humors, the spleen, and so forth, as well as ailments of the eyes and limbs. *Oṃ ratnābarta sarvapāpaṃ harantu maṃ hūṃ | prakṛtakrodha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra is a great mantra, the unsurpassed protection among all protections. Having performed the preliminary ritual in former times, it protects the body of the yogin. [Recite] seven times.

Having offered high praise, one should recite this three times at five locations. Visualizing the five Buddhas, one should empower the crown of the head. This [mantra] destroys lions, enemies, and the like, as well as thieves, fire, water, wind, bile, and other diseases; it overcomes terrifying fears. *Oṃ vimohe sammohe sarvapriye ti hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*. By means of this...

It is taught that the mantra, through its great power, deludes all wandering beings; it generates non-affection and brings about universal attachment. Having rinsed one’s mouth with water from the left hand during the morning hours, the yogin who desires accomplishment will achieve all purposes. Following this, the supreme application is explained: the most excellent essence arising from the essence, the meditation upon the vajra and so forth.

The bird [of wisdom] and [the bird of ignorance] merge non-dually in equality; through this limb, one meditates on their distinction. Even that which is poisonless is struck by poison. By means of extremely unbearable delusion, the deluded yogi himself is terrified. Through the method of the Dharma with diligence, the pure body is made utterly pure. By beholding the Lamp of Purity, the darkness of the afflictions and so forth is destroyed. [This is] the vajra in the sky-vajra.

The mind dissolves completely into the mind; meditating on entities such as the "one" and so forth is the defining characteristic of this yoga. With the remaining fire and so forth, it swirls intensely in the center and further within the center. One should behold the realm of space with that light through perfect meditative equipoise. From the sprout of this seed-syllable, the *āli* and *kāli* emerge; from the seed-syllable, seeds proliferate even throughout the realm of space.

Visualize her dwelling in the pure realm, situated in the center of a sun mandala, in the midst of a vetālī. She sits upon a lotus seat, completely covered by a white parasol. Her two hands are in the bodhisattva posture (*vajraparyaṅka*), her color is red with equal radiance, and she is adorned with three eyes, a hook, a noose, and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). She gazes with a graceful, amorous expression and wears red garments.

Having completely covered [the object], one should visualize the syllables of nectar within the supreme mind and intention; at the tip of the hook is the syllable *kṣūm*. By reciting this, one should draw [it] forth; with the reflected image, one should stir the mind and delight it with one's own breath. *Oṃ rāgara-gata-bhati hūṃ kṣūṃ svāhā*. By means of the mantra and mudrā of the hook, the yogin—

Leading those who desire [liberation], the utterly deluded and the greatly deluded, one should accomplish [this] while in meditative equipoise. From the *Caturpīṭha-tantra*, from the third [chapter on] the seat of application, this is the condensed essence of accomplishment; it is a summary of the summary. Then, with a body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), the yogi in perfect equipoise, with the intention of eating and being eaten, [attains] purification, realization, and the eye.

One should not perform [harmful acts], nor should one regard things as extraordinary, nor should anything be conceptualized. Regarding the classes of beings, high and low, and so forth—the fifth deity is equanimity. One should not mentally cause harm to those who are born and so forth. If one harbors a harmful intent, the yogic vow will be far removed. As for the appropriation of others' property, whether great or small, it is the mind of theft.

One must not do so; the yoga vow is indeed far-reaching. One should abandon for a long time false speech, harsh words, slander, and frivolous talk. Because they harm the minds of others, the yoga vow is indeed far-reaching. By applying oneself thoroughly to the meaning and the *liṅga*, this is the very essence of the dharma of application. Through delusion, with malicious intent, speech, and so forth, one disparages that very application. Well...

Through the karma of what has been done, with a body that generates happiness, and by making the welfare of sentient beings one's primary concern, one trains well in the Mahāyāna. One should not speak unpleasant words that harm sentient beings; one should not perform sinful deeds, nor disparage the yoga-treatises. One should have no craving for the pleasures of yoga, and one should not become intoxicated by delusion. One should be thoroughly skilled in binding the mudrās.

In application, one should rely [on the practice] out of self-interest; through the excellent application of relying and further reliance, the deity is pleased and the accomplishment is achieved. By means of the essence of benefiting sentient beings, one brings benefit through the happiness of sentient beings. This is the great fruit of the Mahāyāna; one should rely upon it by this path. In whatever way one applies oneself, in that very way there is happiness through benefit. Through the vows for sentient beings and so forth, that...

One’s own mind should not be harmed; when born within saṃsāra, one should be perfectly endowed with skillful means and wisdom. One effects both existence and non-existence, and transforms the welfare of sentient beings into the syllable *āḥ*. By binding the seal that possesses the four mudrās—the secret of secrets—ambrosia arises in its center and a sprout emerges. This is the supreme *āḥ*, complete with three petals.

It is infinite; furthermore, the supreme nectar itself is the very essence of all external things. It is the delightful nectar for the fortunate field, and it is taught as pleasant to sentient beings. It is the body of all five Buddhas, blazing like refined gold. With its crown bound and uplifted, and adorned with four arms, it possesses the moods of laughter and grace, and is [decked] with all ornaments.

Adorned [with ornaments], the upper [right hand] holds a vajra-hook and the second a vajra-noose; the left [hands] hold a vajra-bell and, thirdly, an iron chain for binding. These are the mudrās of the four hands, which bind the secret and other [spheres]. With a body and complexion blazing with light, one should rest in meditative equipoise upon Amitābha. The seed-syllable in the form of the letter *Ha* brings about the joy of the supreme syllable. *Hoḥ*.

Through the aspect of *yi*, body and body are the deity Vairocanādhipati. Through the meditation on mind and mental factors, one is fully renowned as the deity itself. It seizes the life-force and mind of all bodies and embodied beings. *Hrīḥ*.

The seed-syllable in the form of *yi* is the great powerful Vajrapāṇi; it clearly becomes the form of *oṃ*, which realizes the mind from all sides. By that form of *ā*, one is satisfied; it is fully taught by the wise one. The goddess of nectar-water is the realization of that which is to be known. Through tasting whatever nectar there is, the fruit of nectar is attained—the joyful deity of the Tathāgatas.

The consort is one of supreme beauty, most enchanting; with the forms of all the Buddhas, the fourth mudrā should be bound. If the yogin desires accomplishment, he should meditate on the two as non-dual. Because the two are both existence and non-existence, they are fully clarified by the one endowed with primordial wisdom. Binding with great pride is binding with a mind possessed of conceptual elaboration; [it is characterized by] grace, wrath, and deportment.

By means of this, she dissolves into the very heart of the goddess; having touched the seat of the Sun’s hand with the hand of the Moon, and having embraced and embraced her, she dissolves into the wisdom of the goddess. One should satisfy the fire-god of the wisdom of the belly in his own place; through the dissolution of Wisdom into Method, one should satisfy them by means of non-dual union. Oṃ ha ho hrīḥ.

Āḥ! This is the seed-syllable of the Great Seed; by means of this, the seed should be visualized. Through this sequence, the offering is not for the sake of medicinal ingredients. The Goddess, who removes hunger and suffering, who is graceful and speaks sweetly, who performs the pride of being without pride, and possesses diligence despite being without exertion—this all-pervading, fortunate Goddess bewilders, terrifies, and summons. She is not... [of the mind].

With dignity and the fear of shame, she conquers with her melodious voice; thus endowed with these qualities, the goddess is lovely, a sweet nectar of pleasant sound. She abides in the state of desire and liberation; whoever follows this path of the goddess possesses the five arts of the *cātaka* bird, the parrot’s speech, and graceful dance. The asuras possess seven types of diligence, while the eighth is the loss of mindfulness. The goddess...

The activity of the eight messengers swiftly captivates the mind. The yogin’s own mind acts with a desire-filled intention. According to the characteristics as they have been taught, one should diligently arrange various parchments. Seated upon a lotus throne, adorned by a solar mandala, the eight messengers appear entirely in the form of women, their colors corresponding to the directions.

And as for the colors: one who possesses the qualities of a beautiful form, with a great conch shell and so forth in hand, [should offer] water of nectar at each respective place. Adorned with vessels of the five meats and so forth, and beautified by food and offerings, the wise one should perform the practice before its reflection. Together with flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth, and properly endowed with the non-dual *tarpaṇa* offering, first of all, the mudrā of the commitment (*samaya*)—

One should bind the king and others; extending the moon-like hand, one is fully endowed with the power of cognition. *Oṃ hili hili hūṃ phaṭ*. By means of the samaya mantra and mudrā, one should apply oneself to the activity of worship: *Oṃ āmr̥takundali ha ho hrīḥ*.

*Āḥ svāhā*: this is the mantra for ritual service (*upacāra*) and the mudrā. Upon the seat of the sun’s hand, with the hands joined like the moon, one should perform one's desired activities through the essence-heart and the mudrā. The yogin should first perform the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth by reciting [the mantra] one million times; thereafter, the activities such as those involving fire are performed through the non-dual *bali* offering. The fire hearth (*agni-kunda*).

In the third [chapter], having thoroughly ignited a firewood of *snang byed* (arka) trees, one should prepare it by anointing it with the flowers of a goddess and honey; then, mixing it thoroughly with nectar-water and correctly grasping the name of whomever [one intends], one should offer eight hundred oblations, and that person will certainly be brought under control. One should offer the ashes of the Fire-god and others, along with one’s own semen, into the center of the nectar five times.

When performed, one brings oneself under control according to one's desire. If one consecrates *madana* (intoxicant), snake, the fifth [ingredient], and *audaja* wood in equal parts together with nectar (*amṛta*), one will quickly become insane. A wise person should perform the practice at the tips of *nimba* and other such trees. Through the ritual of non-dual offerings, including flowers, incense, and perfumes, one should diligently kindle the fire from the root of white *ārga*.

Having thoroughly ignited [the fire], one should grind fine lotus powder and anoint it with milk and nectar. Having performed eight hundred burnt offerings (*homa*), the remaining ashes are distributed. Sprinkled seven times with water from the root of *citraka*, they are dried in the shade. At the time of worship, the yogin quickly sprinkles those ashes with nectar-water; this causes the body to become as white as a *kunda* flower, yet bewildered.

Form, and the scent of extreme delusion and confusion—the goddesses who are the eight messengers—possess power and majesty that are devoid of purpose. For sentient beings deluded by conceptual thought, this ritual action is applied; through it, the yogi who has abandoned delusion will swiftly realize the state of existence. Having prepared this as a medicinal powder (*cūrṇa*), one should discard the *jāti* and the oil three times; this is the offering of nectar (*amṛta*).

At that time, having mixed the ashes together, by tasting the *bindu* with the tongue, one will be seized by the eight messengers (*dūta*). When the signs of the messengers are fully perfected, one becomes insane, intoxicated, and delirious. One should properly take the "insanity-inducing" wood, diligently kindle a fire, and burn flowers, honey, and nectar a hundred times each; from that, the ashes should be taken.

Then, one should perform the preparatory rites and so forth. If that ash is applied to the place where the nectar is generated, the color of the water will change, and its taste will likewise be transformed. By means of honey and butter, its form will become like that of a cluster [of flowers]. Having taken that ash, it should be mixed with a portion of the three bodies (*trikāya*), seven portions of nectar, and eight portions of *maru-tsa*.

Furthermore, at the time of making offerings, if one pours its ashes into the liquor, then by the mere act of giving it to anyone, one will spontaneously know all nectars according to one's own desire. By whichever path [leads] to whichever [state], for the sake of clearing away the delusions of sentient beings through those very paths, one should always teach the way. One should strive for the benefit of others; this is the summary of one’s own desires. [And] medicine...

Furthermore, regarding the application of mantra, it is deficient in wisdom, medicine, and so forth. According to the *Caturpīṭha Tantra*, this is the summary of its essential nature, which extracts the essence of the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the third [chapter], the rite of the *bali* offering. For the purpose of accomplishing mantra, one should thoroughly prepare an image.

By properly applying the supreme image, one accomplishes it through the sequence of blessings. Pacifying, enriching, magnetizing, slaying, expelling, and causing division—all these are accomplished by means of the image. One should fashion the image according to its characteristics: first, the characteristics of the cloth; second, the characteristics of the *tāla* leaf; third, the sequence of colors; and fourth, the ritual offering (*bali*).

Regarding the fire sacrifice itself: having first generated one's own desired intention, one should draw the peaceful mandala upon a cloth that is unblemished, complete with its fringes, and fully expanded with upper and lower borders. One should wear a garment of *preta* (flesh-eating ghost) silk that has not fallen into disrepair and possesses its fringes intact; this is the characteristic of the expansive [rite]. For the red silk of a female *preta*, one should employ that which has not fallen [into disrepair], provided it is not touched by [impure] pigments.

When applied without striking [the target], it is renowned as the very empowerment itself. On the skin of a black goat, or on others such as that of a cow or a horse, the characteristics of the rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*)—which are dark and fierce—are manifested. At the site for its suppression, one should mark the characteristics of the lines; divide them into three parts, cast one part below, and place two parts upon the fifth.

Third, regarding the lines as they were taught: the Brahma-line and the staff-line consist of five parts each, while the body is held to be three parts. The peaceful [face] and the limbs are equal; the face itself consists of twelve parts. The neck is four finger-widths (*aṅgula*), and the head and hair are likewise that same measure. The ears are also of that measurement, and the three parts of the face are the forehead, the throat, and the nose.

The tip of the ear is at the end of the nose; the eyes are two finger-widths [in measure], and the nostrils are four finger-widths—that is the characteristic of the eyes. In the middle of the end of the neck, the chest region is pressed by two [fingers]; it is pressed at the location of the heart and pressed all around at the navel. Pressed at the edge of the breasts, with both breasts pressed against the chest, it is pressed by both hands.

The two [heels] are pressed against each other; they possess four finger-widths. The thighs and calves are fully endowed [with that measure], and the two knees have four finger-widths. The measurement of the feet is likewise. With twelve *tāla* measures, one should draw the form of the deity. The four additional finger-widths serve as the seats for the eight deities; the seat for the ninth is explained to be two finger-widths.

The central lunar mandala is completely surrounded by the light rays of the robes and so forth; the most profound vajra deity itself measures twelve *tāla* [palms] in height. On the lower portion and its subdivisions, one should draw the *re-mo* patterns such as the *upacitra* and others. On the remaining upper portion, the five families are shown. One should accomplish the deity according to one's desire, with colors and so forth corresponding to the activity. The reflection is clearly...

The preliminary application consists of twelve *tāla* units. Regarding the measurement of those *tāla*s: having drawn both arms inward from all sides, one should exclude two finger-widths (*aṅgula*) for the form of a peaceful deity. From that [measurement], the face should be made according to the *tāla*; the belly should be large and expansive, and one should exclude two finger-widths from every joint and every section. [This applies to] the wrathful male and female deities, the *Īśvarī*, and the minor male and female servants.

As for the instructions: one should draw ten fierce and terrifying figures upon ten palm leaves. One who desires to accomplish the mandala should include the offering goddesses; the eighth part of the cloth should be placed upon the palm leaves. The sequence of the goddesses of the mandala should be arranged layer by layer. In the center is the sovereign deity Vajra, characterized as being singular.

If the throat, the *kos-ko*, and the feet themselves—these three—are long, it is a fault. For a practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*), it certainly brings about one's own expulsion and the destruction of one's dwelling. If the nose, the ears, and the fingers—these three—are short, the fault is the certain destruction of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) and the long-term loss of one's glory. If the neck, the calves, and the cheeks—these three—are thick, it is a great fault. I...

As for the nature of the practitioner himself: the demon, the obstacle-maker, and the long-lived one—if these three are low on the cheeks, the chest, and the sides of the ribs, there is great fault; wealth will be destroyed very soon, without delay. If these three—the breasts, the ears, and the forehead—are high, there is great merit; the practitioner will quickly fall into strife and be harmed by enemies. As for the chest, the body, and the two thighs...

If these three are low, there is great fault: one will be terrified by enemies and will undoubtedly even face death. With a depressed nose, wandering eyes, and ears, lips, and forehead, one is threatened by obstacles, Māras, and fire, and spiritual accomplishments will remain far away. With upward-looking breath, a shifting and unstable seat, and defects in the chest, throat, and limbs—these are faults.

The number is known to be immeasurable; with flickering rays of light and [faulty] hand gestures and implements, the image of the practitioner suffers the pain of the torment of sorrow. Regarding the defects of the three types of narrowness—of the backrest, the parasol, and the seat—the faults are death, the ruin of glory, and the destruction of friends and the loss of those who are not friends. Thus are the great faults of these defects.

Tamed and disciplined, possessing patience, with a mind in perfect meditative equipoise, one should engage in conceptualization and thorough investigation. Having perfected all characteristics, one demonstrates worship through a beautiful manner. Regarding the purpose of accomplishing mantras, the deities for empowerment and summoning, and for pacifying, one employs a peaceful manner; for wrathful rites, one is fierce and terrifying, heroic and possessing the pride of a hero.

Laughing, wrathful, and playful, manifesting in the form of a wrathful deity, and appearing as male and female servants, one should transform one’s own complexion according to the site and location of the ritual activity. By thus characterizing these features, the mantrin shall quickly accomplish the siddhis according to the yogin’s desires; [therefore] one should paint a mandala on a cloth. *namaḥ samantabuddhānām*.

*Sambodhani viśuddhā namaḥ sarvabhīghare namtu hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.* By means of this mantra, the mantrin shall wash the cloth and the thread. With the mantra of all activities, which is blessed by the five Buddhas, the practitioner shall prepare the painting (*paṭa*) by applying each individual image. As the cause for the accomplishment of the images, one should offer...

One should perform the fire-offering mudrā and mantra. Having taken the garments of the pretas, one should diligently prepare eight thangkas endowed with torma offerings and the like. The painting should be executed using colored threads. Seated upon a lotus throne, positioned in the center of a moon mandala, he sits in the sattvaparyaṅka posture. The two hands are beautifully adorned with the *thang ga* [ornament]; the vajra crown has a topknot at its peak; the Buddha...

Adorned with the five [ornaments], his body decorated with every kind of ornament; wrapped in silks that flow and flutter, he brandishes a vajra with his hand and exerts himself supremely in pressing it to his heart. With a bell manifest in his left hand, he presses it against the junction of his waist. With the complexion of refined gold, a graceful and exceedingly smiling face, he rests upon the vajra-mandala.

Furthermore, wrathful rays of light radiate forth; white with the color of the moon and the *kunda* flower, the goddess holds a secret vessel. Embraced by his feet, she joins her palms; with both hands she embraces his throat. Pressing her lips against his teeth, she is intoxicated by the supreme wrathful one. His body is adorned with ornaments, and he wears garments of passion; from his crown protrudes a vajra.

Furthermore, this King Vajreśvara, completely covered by a white parasol, possesses a lotus body and holds a vajra. In the eastern quarter, he is depicted in human form; all his physical features and so forth are fully developed. This sovereign Yakṣī sits upon a jeweled throne, adorned with every ornament, and holds in her hand a vessel for *bali* offerings and other such items.

One should refine [the materials] into the colors of the directions. The goddess who bestows all accomplishments is the sister of Kūbera. Bowing with a gesture of homage is the characteristic of accomplishing the goddess. On the northern side is the goddess who speaks pleasantly; thus is the King Vajreśvara, the Lotus-bodied Jñānadhara, with the color of refined, beautiful gold. Good.

Seated upon the throne, adorned with all the ornaments, holding vessels of nectar in two hands, the wise one should depict her looking with an expression of grace. In the western direction is the goddess Śrīvasundharā, with a complexion like refined gold, adorned with all the ornaments, a youthful goddess whose every characteristic is fully perfected.

Now, as for the accomplishment: her second hand is adorned with vessels such as the five hooks; in the southern quarter is the one named Bhūtī, wearing a sash; blue in color and beautiful in form, she is fully adorned with all ornaments; in her two hands she holds a vessel of nectar; she possesses the limbs of another’s grace; she is indeed the sister of Yama, the bestower of all accomplishments.

The goddess, with a beautiful form for all [beings], should be visualized and painted as a mandala; likewise, the vajra, bell, and so forth should be arranged in order starting from the northeast (Īśāna). With two hands in the *vīrāsana* posture, her hands bearing mudrās, symbols, and so on—in this way, one should contemplate the playful wheel of the King Vajreśvara. The deities, together with their objects of focus, are accompanied by mantras and mudrās.

Offer with the *bali* cake: *oṃ sarvasiddhi kuru hūṃ*. This is the mantra for the services (*upacāra*). *Oṃ vajra hūṃ phaṭ*. With the right hand fully extended, press down upon the wisdom lotus; this is the samaya mantra and mudrā. By means of that mantra and mudrā, one should protect the six limbs. Having bound the two wisdom fists, hold the white [substance] and the earth-umbrella upright, swirling [them].

Having embraced her with the parasol mudrā, one should summon her with the white iron hook: *oṃ vajrāṅkuśa jaḥ*. Firmly binding that same mudrā, join the white [hook] and the *gīvaṅga*; through the binding mudrā of the noose, the goddess is present everywhere. *oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ*. Having firmly bound that same mudrā, one should join back-to-back; it is secret and most secret.

With the iron chain of the waist, one should please all the deities. Having firmly bound that very fist, join it back-to-back. By linking the earth, the parasol, and the lotus, one completely satisfies the deity. With the two hands endowed with incense, extend both fingers upright; by abiding as the moon and sun, this is the mudrā of great compassion. Oṃ suratavajra.

HŪṂ JAḤ. Having bound the two fists and joined them palm-to-palm above the sun, this is the heart mantra and mudrā of the goddess of the eastern direction: OṂ ŚRĪYE VATI HŪṂ PHUḤ SVĀHĀ. Binding that same mudrā as a seal, with the wisdom and consciousness fingers raised: OṂ SURTIMA (? HŪṂ PHUḤ SVĀHĀ. This is the heart mantra of the goddess of the northern direction.

This is the mudrā. Having bound that very mudrā into its seal, with the white [hand] and the *giwang* held upright: *oṃ suru suru madure hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the heart mantra and mudrā of the goddess of the western direction. Having bound that very mudrā into its seal, one should join the earth, the parasol, and the lotus: *oṃ priye mekhalā hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the goddess Rājādhipatī of the southern direction.

The essence is the mantra and the mudrā. With the mantra of the non-dual ritual, the wise one should perform worship. With incense, flowers, and so forth, as well as songs, the wise one should worship with the twenty-fold offering. The source of virtue for desire and liberation, which accomplishes all activities, the blissful Vajradharma—this is accomplished through the yoga-mantra. Then, the essence of all...

The wrathful Gnod byed and the wrathful goddesses are the very nature of the three types of division; they emanate as the supreme wrathful deities of the four branches of the Buddha’s awakening. Through the gaze of the goddesses, they terrify the three types of fearful vehicles. They sever the māras and elemental spirits, parch the māras and the obstructors, suppress them, and expel them from their domains, [bestowing] the state of desire and liberation.

One should accomplish the subjugation and destruction of Brahmā, the forceful summoning of Cāmuṇḍī, and the complete accomplishment of Bhairava; these should be accomplished by the wise. First, one should draw the image exactly as it has been described in its characteristics: fourteen crores [of deities], possessing various forms and ugly countenances, with the Goddess Durgā as the seat, adorned with all ornaments and draped in many cloths.

In the center of the solar mandala, Vajradāka is manifested, possessing three faces and six arms. His faces blaze with blue light; upon a seat increased by his play, he tramples the head of Brahmā with his feet. With three eyes and a wrathful expression, he possesses eyes that are red and reddish-brown. His hair is tawny, swirling and joyfully disheveled.

Adorned with a garland of bone skulls, he wears the Buddha as a formidable crown; he is further embellished by two nāgas visualized as the heads of obstructors. Laughing loudly with bared fangs, he has three faces of three different colors. He bears an elephant hide and is clothed in human skin. Upon the very sites of his eight ornaments are white, blazing bones. The Buddha...

[He wears] a garland of heads, has sharp fangs and blazing fingers, and in his upper [hands] he holds an arrow; in the second, a *khaṭvāṅga*; and with the third, he brandishes a vajra. His right hands hold a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a noose, while the second holds a skull-cup; the third is fully equipped with a bow. He tramples upon the fierce and terrifying Jaraṇḍa, who is bound by a noose and adorned [with ornaments]. He suppresses the Fierce One.

With bared fangs, dripping blood, and fainting, when they are individually adorned in the center, each one accomplishes its own messenger. Constantly and uninterruptedly exerting themselves, clothed in the seven colors, they possess the blazing light-rays and vajras of the wrathful deities with bared fangs. [They are] covered by human skeletons and white parasols; [this is] the Lord of Wisdom Wrathful Deities.

I am fierce and extremely fierce, the subduer who overcomes all Māras. Since extremely malevolent sentient beings cannot be tamed through peaceful means, I manifest forms such as wrathful deities through the union of skillful means and wisdom. Crows, hawks, vultures, owls, rākṣasas, dogs, and the like let out terrifying cries; [there is] that which is filled with human skeletons.

Thus, by means of the application of the image (*pratimā*), the mantra practitioner who seeks both worldly desires and liberation should accomplish the image that terrifies all wrathful ones with the mantra: *oṃ tāṃ hūṃ matha matha duṣṭān ghātaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. By means of the mudrās of the three banners and so forth, one thoroughly performs all activities. Possessing all the fragrant offerings such as incense and perfumes, along with the extensive offerings, [one should proceed].

One who possesses the offerings for the heroes and so forth, and has seen the ritual of the mandala, should perform the *bali* rite as a specific branch of the fire-offering (*homa*) ritual. Even with unexamined meat and blood, one should satisfy [the deity] in that very manner, according to whatever siddhi one desires. *Oṃ avatīrṇi mahākrodha hūṃ phaṭ*. Having extended the moon and sun, [one places them] on the back.

One should join them at the front and the back; having joined the white *gi-wang*, one joins the earth-disk (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*) and the lotus. That very heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) and that very mantra are to be purified. As for the placement of the ritual pegs (*kīla*), the fences, the nets, the armor, and the weapons in the place of activity, this mudrā is renowned as the best. This very mudrā is bound at the heart; [it is] primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

First, one should join it with consciousness: *oṃ kro dha ni hūṃ āḥ*. One should clearly manifest the seed-syllable of the supreme essence and that very mudrā. Without regard for body or life, one should accomplish it with a great mind. A fierce and sharp goddess is to be accomplished with a sharp mind; a slightly peaceful goddess has the characteristic of a single method. In a place on the bank of water...

One should first perform the preliminary service (*sevā*) and so forth; five hundred thousand recitations are required, followed by one hundred thousand. Having presented peaceful offerings, one should perform the fire rituals (*homa*) and so on. Mixing the flesh of a black goat with blood, one should perform the burnt offering according to the complete ritual procedure before an image such as a painted scroll (*paṭa*). One should satisfy [the deities] with the *bali* offering and the burnt offering; thus, all activities [are accomplished].

Success will be achieved; pacifying, enriching, magnetizing, and wrathful rites, as well as the practice of sorcery and so forth, will be accomplished. By means of extensive offerings with vases filled with fragrant water, for those afflicted by the limbs of disease;

Having first bestowed empowerment and grace, one will attain the pacification of all diseases, as well as the very harm caused by planetary spirits, and all [afflictions] arising from misfortune and lack of affection. From yellow pigment and human fat, one should fashion an image of a deity in the form of a *vināyaka* (obstructing spirit), seated upon an even throne with palms joined, adorned with four arms, bared fangs, and full limbs.

Residing within a lotus vessel, holding a trident and a food vessel, and piercing with a battle-axe held in hand; measuring four finger-widths and adorned with all ornaments—this yantra should be drawn before an image of a painted icon, using *guggulu* and saffron on birch bark or tree bark, depicting the form of the practitioner.

Endowed with all aspects, one should write the name in the heart; together with the hook that moves, falls, and draws forth the life-force, it should be drawn up and placed upon the forehead. Having pressed down upon the seat of the Lord of Obstacles at the heart, one should place it there. One should worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, and with diligence perform the rite of the *bali* offering. The yogin who seeks the fruit of abandoning worldly aims [should act thus].

Recite the mantra syllables: *oṃ trām thā thā thā hūṃ jaḥ svāhā*. While reciting this over white flowers, one should strike [the target] with each one. When the one hundred and eight repetitions are complete, there is no doubt that success will be achieved. By means of this application of the mantra, the practitioner’s mind will be moved, and [the target] will be swiftly summoned and brought. This applies even to powerful kings, lords, and the like. And as for kings...

If, through mere desire, the regents, the children of the wealthy and so forth, bodies of exquisite beauty, Śakra and others, as well as meat and wine, were all brought under the power of the practitioner simply by his will, they would remain perpetually submissive for as long as the body lives. Through pride—the foremost of the limbs of pride—one will achieve success. By manifesting the form of a wrathful deity, one’s activities and rites will be swiftly accomplished.
The "Manifestation of the Wrathful Body" is hereby complete.

The characteristics of conduct encompass all phenomena; they are firm in their defining marks. Those who desire the fruit of enjoying primordial wisdom should understand the characteristics of conduct. The terrors of unbearable saṃsāra consist in falling into existence through attachment. With a body that has abandoned attachment, one should constantly maintain the ascetic observances (*vrata*). By remaining in profound meditative equipoise in solitude, all things are summarized in brief.

Through attachment one falls into existence; through craving one enters into saṃsāra. Having long abandoned the nature of delusion, for the sake of teaching the Dharma to sentient beings, even though one acts for the benefit of sentient beings, accomplishment comes through secluded application and ascetic vows that are difficult to endure. One wanders in the ocean of the faults of attachment; therefore, in order to conquer the afflictions of the self, [one acts] for the benefit of sentient beings.

The mind alone understands; when the time comes to benefit sentient beings, one acts according to the previous conduct and vows. Free from the bustle of society, one dwells in solitude and guards the body with joy. First, the yogi takes up the words of the treatises and, being perfectly endowed with all the vows, practices the Dharma with great sharpness of intellect. Never at any time does he dwell even upon states or non-states.

One should accept [alms]; one should not discriminate between what is edible and what is inedible, nor should one fixate on whether [the donor] is low-born or otherwise. With constant joy through diligent effort, one should always beg for alms by means of a mind that regards the cobbler, the fisherman, the butcher, the brahmin, the commoner, and the kṣatriya as equal. Furthermore, if while practicing as described above, one should eat at a banquet or receive bedding, clothing, or spittoons...

Furthermore, merely by abiding in the vow of delightful enjoyments, the yogic discipline is far-reaching. The yogin should take merit into his own hands through the nine modes of conduct; though he takes everything, there is no fault, for he does not grasp at things as real entities. For one whose mind is utterly pure, everything is food and indeed edible; being pure and full of devotion, I—

The King said: "One should completely abandon that place; however, for the purpose of drawing a mandala with faith, or for the rites of *bali* offerings, one should present the accumulated substances at that location. As for the remains of the three religious robes (*tricīvara*), they should again be held with reverence. Upon the crown of the head are the signs of the saffron robe, the limbs of the Buddha’s enlightenment, and the essential inner vestment along with the three religious robes."

On top [of the staff] is a vajra, along with a bell and a water-strainer for the forearm; on the body holding these, there are no other items such as books. To ward off ants and the like, a small gong is recommended. The branches of the Buddha’s enlightenment, the root of the Dharma’s meaning—compassion itself—and the training thereafter are the vows of the Guru’s word. The Buddha...

Vast wisdom and great miraculous power, supreme refuge and object of refuge; to Vajreśvara of supreme form, to Vajrasattva, I prostrate. To the five ḍākinīs, whose nature is the union with the goddess Prajñā, I prostrate. Oṃ amuka samayo haṃ samaya | amuka samayo haṃ samaya | Oṃ vajra vajra | mahāvajra vajra.

*Kāyasupara, hi hi hi, ho ho ho, hūṃ nani patadam.* One should thoroughly accept this disciple; through the second activity, one should accomplish the Vajra-vow-holder. By means of the application and the secret mantra-vidyā, at all times and at the very moment, these two verses should be recited: "Whoever is father, whoever is mother, and whoever is friend—all are impermanent. *Sangs*...

The body of the Victor is indeed an illusion, always fully protected by the Dharma. Alas! By the power of emptiness, all things are utterly subdued. This should be grasped by the wise who bestow the fruit of Buddhahood. For the sake of cutting through delusion, these verses are recited throughout the three times—while walking, sleeping, moving, sitting, and in all states of going.

Having stabilized the application of mantra, one should sleep with mind and mental factors. Through the conduct of day and night, the sins of the body composed of the five elements—transmitted through the succession of generation and birth—are purified. By practicing for six months, one’s own desired deity is accomplished. Even through ignorance, the yogi who practices the ascetic observances (*vrata*) attains primordial wisdom. That...

Thus, the nature of qualities is the field, and the practice of ascetic observances is the cause. Through the application of ascetic observances, all delusion is utterly abandoned. Having perfected the view of equality by means of that which characterizes the nature of skillful methods, there remains only the perfectly pure view. By the flavor of universal emptiness and equality, all things are devoid of characteristics.

At the limit of universal emptiness, whatever conceptualizations have been imagined and discriminated by delusion—the pure mind and mental factors, the body that is an ocean of delusive afflictions, and that basis of desire and wrath—[are all subsumed therein]. Through the sharp mind, the deluded one [realizes] the distinction of the body endowed with primordial wisdom. [One experiences] the food of striking and soft garments, the various touches of Indra.

Through the perversion caused by the attachment of delusion, one performs actions that lead to rebirth in existence (*bhava*). Karma becomes the sovereign of what is to be done; the ignorance of the deluded is impermanent wisdom. It destroys desire, anger, and pride; it is the food for death within existence. One should have compassion for beings and their origins, and never contemplate evil. For those who are protectorless, suffering, and destitute, through error they fall into the Avīci hell, as if [falling] from the world...

On this support, the primary things are jesting and mockery; yet, through being well-trained in the Mahāyāna, one does not even become a being of the lower realms. By eating everything—whether coarse or fine—with perfect joy, one protects the body. Through the poor food of old feasts, one should certainly make oneself happy; [one should also maintain] the training of former vows and so forth, having previously prepared for all of them.

Through the practice of ascetic observances (*vrata*) in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), one does not perceive even the Avīci hell. By means of indicating the characteristics of the past, one should train in the preliminary trainings and so forth. Through the practice of ascetic observances in meditative equipoise, one should train with reverence in the precepts. [One should visualize] a woman of terrifying and fierce form, with hair tied up and curled, wearing soft red funeral shrouds, and covered in fine dust.

Dividing the flesh, even that made from human bone, the woman is adorned with various ornaments; the old red quilted garment is covered with human skin. Holding two great vessels as the second [set], one grasps the five sense organs. Above, the vajra-staff is adorned with the bones of human limbs; the banner and the garland of bells are held in the left hand. Thus it is summarized.

With this body, one should practice ascetic observances with diligence; for in this way, one must not touch substances and other things that are like a blazing fire. One should not even collect other items such as food and drink at first; rather, with a mind of compassion and benefit, one should eat with total joy. Since all [other] things are useless and harmful, one should completely abandon them; thus, the body is protected.

With just that much, one should beg for food; one should dwell in empty houses, cemeteries, the outskirts of villages, and in forests. One should wander everywhere at night, characterized by supreme recitation and meditative concentration. Whether walking, sleeping, or sitting—with a mind that is transparent and whose nature is utterly pure—recitation and meditative concentration are exclusively that. By means of that, all...

That all shall be accomplished has been taught by all the Buddhas; by one who has abandoned sin and acts with discernment, there is no remaining in saṃsāra. Always viewing all things as non-existent with the mind, one then recites two verses regarding the cause of becoming a Buddha oneself: "One should protect through the Dharma of generosity."

One should grant [permission] with a single verse: "Alas! By the power of delusion, all embodied beings are completely brought under control. Because of the fierce phenomena of desire and so forth, the wise have utterly abandoned them. Neither non-existent nor existent, and free from the conceptualization of grasper and grasped, one crosses over the wilderness of existence and attains the bliss of non-referentiality. [This is] the enjoyment imagined by others."

In the three periods of sleeping, walking, and so forth, a single verse of yoga cuts through the delusion of the yogi. With the old cloth accumulated from the mind of the Great Mind, one is thoroughly clad in that garment; holding the beautiful staff of all the skeletal limbs, one beats with the Dharma of the *pataha* drum and takes up the vajra song for the sake of sentient beings.

For the sake of liberation, one wanders from village to village; through the nature of non-referentiality, one remains in meditative equipoise by practicing the ascetic observances (*vrata*). Since the pure mind is non-referential, it should be guarded with joy. Because conduct serves as the cause, the practice of yoga is the cause of the ultimate goal. Having completely cleared away all sins and abandoned all faults, [one practices] the moon-like observance.
By practicing the six [observances], the wisdom of one’s own desire will be accomplished.
This concludes the chapter entitled "The Exposition of the Conduct of Vows.
Then, as for the essence of all things, it is the summary of the meaning of reality itself; it is applied as the essence of all that is stable and moving within cyclic existence.

First, for a time, the yogin, having sat upon a comfortable seat in a pleasing location, should perform the preliminary service and so forth. By means of the vajra or wisdom yoga, he should perform three hundred thousand recitations; thereafter, there is no doubt that his desired activity will be accomplished. One should fashion an image from human fat and anoint it with hot clarified butter.

Having placed the name upon the heart, one should fill the joints and the interstices with thorns. Mixing sour, pungent, and *maru* roots together with an image, one should place them correctly in a vessel. One should then press down upon the body of the wisdom-being with the right foot. By reciting with a sharp mind, there is no doubt that success will be achieved at the end of a single night. It ripens.

One should place [the target] upon the fire; the king will quickly be tormented. For those who cause harm to the Three Jewels, this ritual action should be applied: *hrīḥ āmo ghasi sida ha da ha gri hna gri hna hūṃ hrīḥ*. At the time of sunrise in the morning, one should perform the pacifying fire sacrifice (*śāntika-homa*) according to the ritual for white flowers, incense, and lamps.

In a vessel containing a mixture of water and milk, having prepared a *bali* offering therein, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; thus the king will be freed from illness. *Oṃ āmṛtavārade hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ā ā ā*. Having gathered everything together, one should cast it into the current of a great river.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Thorough Pacification of Epidemic Diseases."

Then, the practitioner of mantra should thoroughly employ this essence-mantra (*hṛdaya*). One should fashion an image from white mustard seeds, and the name [of the target] should be joined to the heart. With a stone or thorns placed upon the navel, one should step upon it with the foot while reciting: *sutikṣṇāśulahuṃ vajra phaṭ hrīḥ*. One should heat and torment it over fire, and especially recite while remaining there. Thus, as indicated...

By means of its characteristic, it seizes again because of the immediate piercing. From the ritual procedure for the offering of peace: if one washes with milk and honey and sends [it] away on the current of a river, one will be free from the disease of piercing pain. *Oṃ sarvakāri hūṃ ja svāhā*. This is the mantra that pacifies piercing pain. Then, by means of the essence of all, the characteristic of another rite is as follows: previously...

By performing the services such as *sevā* and so forth, all activities will be accomplished. At the end of the dark fortnight, from the dung of a dried cow, one should fashion the name and image of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Anoint it with red sandalwood and place the name of the person to be acted upon all over it. Pressing the eyeballs with a *khadira* wood stake using the left foot, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while offering incense into the fire.

By fumigating with incense, the eyes will be seized by piercing pain. *Oṃ cakṣu-maṇi hūṃ phaṭ*. Through this mantra and its ritual application, there is no doubt that success will be achieved. Having performed worship with peaceful offerings, one should recite *oṃ vajratīkṣṇāya hūṃ svāhā* seven times with clear praise. If one bathes [the eyes] with the flow of that [liquid], it will eliminate the diseases and harms of the subject to be accomplished—the eyes.

This is the ritual procedure called "The Eye Disease that Becomes Sharp and Clear," which pacifies eye ailments. One should accomplish it with thorns; the wise one should draw [the design] with blood. Having applied poison and charcoal from a cremation ground to the pupil of the eye, one should stand upon it with the left foot and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times: *oṃ kṛṣṇapiṅgali hūṃ khaṃ phaṭ*. This is its mantra.

By means of the mantra, one should humble oneself with a sense of weightiness; thus, through the possession of all characteristics, the object of accomplishment will quickly become blind. Having anointed [the eyes] with honey and clarified butter, it removes the diseases and harms of the object of accomplishment. Reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times: *oṃ amṛtalocane āḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra for completely pacifying blindness. Furthermore, the practitioner [should act] toward the object of accomplishment...

One should thoroughly practice this; one will not be stained by the sin of harming the Three Jewels. Taking a lotus-shaped vessel made from a skull, one should place the name of the target in its very center. Filling the hollow with dog hair and anointing it with hot clarified butter, one should step upon it with the left foot and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times: *oṃ vajrabaka hūṃ phaṭ*. [Recite] over fire.

By means of heating the field, one should quickly reverse the *bhaga*; this rite is to be applied for an extremely fierce wife. Having recited it seven times with praise, she should be washed with a stream of honey and milk. *Oṃ sukobhavi hūṃ he svāhā*. This is the mantra for pacification. One should take a vessel of clay and fashion it in the shape of a lotus; [fill it with] sharp sesame oil.

One should fill the cavity with white mustard seeds and apply [the remedy]; pressing down with the left foot, one should strike it with a khadira-wood stake. When eight hundred recitations of the mantra have been completed, the bhaga will be tormented and continue to be tormented. *Hrīḥ bilata hūṃ phaṭ*. By means of this mantra and its ritual application, the very act of tormenting the bhaga is accomplished. One should wash it with water and milk, and apply the mantra directly.

One should recite: *oṃ sarvaśodhani svāhā*. By means of this mantra and its ritual application, one is liberated from the affliction of the *bhaga* and other such ailments. Furthermore, the characteristics of the ritual action are to be practiced by the supreme yogin. One should take soil from the path of a king, or else soil from a crossroads; these are the characteristics of the lotus. Then, there is the essence of the *bhaga*, blood, and the mudrā of the preta-mudrā.

Recite this one hundred and eight times: *Hrīḥ Pri Phaṭ*. By means of this mantra and its recitation, it becomes the activity of the Lotus Commitment (*Padmasamvara*). *Oṃ āmrita vati svāhā*. One will not be defiled by the sin of harming the Three Jewels, reviling the guru or the preceptor, or mocking those who practice the commitments (*samaya*).
If one acts out of delusion and anger, having constantly performed [unwholesome] actions, the Buddha has declared without doubt that this will certainly lead to downfall.
The chapter entitled "The Classification of Actions" is complete.

The secret and most secret reality, the supreme essence summarized here, is the reality of liberation—the state of the goal—found within songs such as the *Nāṭyaśāstra*. Since the nature of non-dual reality is free from subject and object, how could there be grasping and a grasper? Because dualistic entities are not the self, dualistic entities are non-existent. Regarding that which is neither an entity nor a non-entity, who is it that, with a mind viewing equanimity, [perceives]...?

Without support or that which is supported, conceptualization and discursive thought are errors; form and the possessor of form are brought to exhaustion. This very nature, which is devoid of intrinsic existence, is the stable ground established by the mind. One should practice meditation, the object of meditation, and the act of meditating. This very nature, which is without focal points, causes all things to dissolve into the basic expanse (*dhātu*). It is the emptiness of emptiness and so forth, reaching the limits of the realm of space.

The nature of reality itself is pure, subtle, and the most subtle of meanings; together with mind and mental factors, because all things are devoid of substantiality, everything is encompassed by space. Constant, eternally constant, and the meaning of permanence—by means of a mind as stable as the element of space—the sparks, atoms, and limbs radiate forth. Like a waterfowl, the remaining consciousness and primordial wisdom (jñāna) of conceptualization radiate and appear within space.

Likewise, having destroyed that darkness of the afflictions with the vajra of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), consciousness blazes forth together; one will attain the manifestation of primordial wisdom and so forth. With the mind, mental factors, and volition, one views and thoroughly engages. Fearless and without harm, one should meditate on entity through entities. Illuminating everything everywhere, it gathers all rays of light.

The seed-syllable of the essence is white, with the color of a *kunda* flower or the moon; through the excellent union of *āli* and *kāli*, this extracted supreme seed-syllable is meditated upon by the yogi in equanimity as the cause for accomplishing the application. By radiating the seed-syllable into space, the three worlds are illuminated; it emanates like clouds without exception, and in an instant, it is both projected and withdrawn. Thereafter, one’s own desire [is fulfilled].

One should further contemplate that which is without objective referent and without syllables. By means of the mind contemplating the equality of form as being empty, and by observing it in its entirety, one illuminates the three realms. Through such mental contemplation, one will come to see the stages of awakening. In an instant, form and form-ness; in an instant, the aspects of the aggregates; in an instant, all shapes.

Therefore, that which is the impermanent state, designated as "well-done" or "ill-done," should not be censured for its faults. Between form and emptiness, and so forth, the mind and mental factors are clearly delineated. Since all remaining entities are non-existent, their remainder is formless. By the blazing lines of primordial wisdom, the rays of light abide in equanimity; this is the very definition that characterizes it.

Practiced by the yogi, it is eternally peaceful and the supreme activity; it is the permanence of perfect enlightenment. Seated upon a comfortable seat in a pleasing location, having first undertaken the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), all activities and purposes are perfectly accomplished. Visualizing the entire Mount Meru at its peak, one’s own desired celestial palace (*vimāna*) of the Great King [of Gods], composed of various supreme jewels and bells...

Adorned with earrings, and further embellished by a white parasol, banners, and various offerings, the very essence of Vajrasattva possesses the radiance of white jasmine and the moon; he is adorned with every ornament and arrayed with the five Buddhas. Wearing most beautiful garments, he holds a vajra and bell in his two hands, emitting manifold rays of light in all directions.

From this, vajra rays of light radiate; the forms of the three realms are meditated upon by the mind and through the mind. Abiding in the center of the mandala at the heart is a blazing red *hūṃ*; at the crown of the head is a drop (*bindu*) like a mountain of fire, radiating from the pores of the skin. A vajra is placed in the east, an arrow is arranged in the south, a sword is marked in the west, and a bow is correctly positioned in the north.

One should place the four [deities], such as Vajrapāśa and the rest, in the intermediate directions and at the corners. Thus, possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, one should meditate with perfect composure. The primary seed-syllable of the *āli* (vowels), endowed with that very reality, should be recited as the mantra. Concluding with the homage and the fire-offering (*homa*), through three hundred thousand recitations of the preliminary service (*sevā*), one’s vajra-body and very self become Vajrasattva.

One becomes equal to the first [Vajrasattva], the hidden essence, the heart-essence, Vajradharma, and Dharmottama. One should perform the subsequent worship of Vajrasattva through the form of the *hūṃ* song. With melodious and auspicious sounds, one should receive [the blessing] while remaining in meditative equipoise. *tribhubabavanajālītamūrtiranurāyanavati rasmi sama hasratīkṣṇadhāsa suparasuparasvavati bahu*.
*Vidāruṇapeśānu rāya nata tatatavati, natei vajrasaparavesaralimalavati svāhā*.
From the extensive *Caturpīṭha-tantra*, this twelve-thousand-verse [work] has been condensed;
from that condensation of the subject matter, this is the further condensation of the essence.
"Free from prosody, grammar, conceptualization, and the like, it is the perfect synthesis of meaning and meaning;
the hidden meaning of the yoga-practice is explained through symbolic language.
From the *Caturpīṭha*, the explanation of the Mantra-portion of the Compendium, titled "The Yoga Maṇḍala," is complete.

The seventh chapter, titled "The Explanatory Tantra of the Mantra Āṃsa," was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Gayādhara and the chief editor-translator ’Gos Khug pa Lhas btsas.
